newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn government under pressure over Nazi pensions.
newsitem.headline: Bonn government under pressure over Nazi pensions.

text.p: The German government came under pressure to justify its actions on Friday after it admitted paying convicted Nazi war criminals "supplementary pensions" while many of the victims had never received any compensation.

Germany's Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis slammed the payments as a "scandal" that brought the country's legal system into disrepute and opposition parties called on the government to pass swift new legislation to stop the practice.

A television network said on Thursday that billions of marks (dollars) were being paid each year to thousands of Nazi war criminals who suffered a disability linked to World War Two on top of their normal pensions.
A Labour Ministry spokesman confirmed the victims' pensions are paid to anyone whose health was impaired by the war living in Germany and that convicted war criminals were no exception.

Bubis told German radio it was bad enough that former SS officers and their dependents were receiving extra wartime pensions. But he said he was horrified that there was no special provision to exclude those convicted of war crimes.

"It's depressing when you realise hundreds of Holocaust survivors from the Vilnius and Riga ghettos (in Lithuania and Latvia) were not eligible because they lived in the former Soviet Union, while their (German) guards were," he said.
"This is absolutely scandalous," he added. "I don't know if it's possible under the current legal system to stop payments to these people...this sort of thing brings our legal system into disrepute."
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens joined forces to call on the government to examine the possibility of withdrawing these special "victims' pensions".

The parliamentary news service HIB said the Greens had asked the government to reveal just how many convicted war criminals were receiving such "victims' pensions" and to redress the imbalance by compensating their victims fully.

Their call was reported a day after the first reading of a new Greens draft law aimed at ensuring 13,000 Jewish Holocaust survivors in eastern Europe receive the same benefits as their counterparts in the West.
They argued that these victims were entitled to a maximum of 1,000 marks ($600) in one-off payments each, while those in Germany received 500 marks ($300) a month.
"The payment of billions from taxpayers money to Nazi and war criminals is a deep humiliation for Holocaust victims," said Otto Schily, the SPD's deputy leader in parliament.
"The perpetrators are doing better than the victims."

The NDR television documentary said on Thursday that about 50,000 war criminals and members of army units that took part in atrocities were receiving war disability pensions ranging from several hundred to several thousand marks each month.
A Bonn spokesman said there were no legal means for the Labour Ministry to stop payments to the war criminals who lived in Germany. He said he did not know how much they received.
"After a long and controversial debate, the German parliament decided in 1950 that all Germans injured in the war had a right to compensation," he told a news conference.

"Lawmakers made no exception in the law. There was discussion whether Nazi war criminals or human rights violators should be excluded. But they agreed it was the task of the justice authorities to deal with war criminals," he said.
The spokesman said only convicted Nazi war criminals living abroad were not entitled to these pensions because they no longer came under German jurisdiction.
